description: We are a team of students from Igor Sikorsky Kyiv Polytechnic Institute with a background in applied physics and programming. We enjoy turning real space and Earth-observation data into tools that people can actually use. Our goal at NASA Space Apps is to combine solid physics with clean code to build a practical, well-tested solution, and to learn as much as possible along the way.
summary:
Earth Analog Explorer is an interactive web tool that finds and ranks places on Earth that best reproduce conditions at Mars landing sites and future lunar south-pole bases.

We built a similarity index from eight measurable criteria: mean surface temperature, temperature range, crater density, slope, relief, ground ice, Sun elevation and rock type. It compares 12 Earth sites (the Namib Desert, the McMurdo Dry Valleys, Devon and Ellesmere islands, Mistastin crater) with Jezero, Gale, Phoenix, Shackleton and Malapert, using open NASA data. A 3D globe, radar charts and pair comparisons show where each analog matches and where it falls short.
We don’t stop at ranking. A “Close the gap” simulator shows which interventions bring a site closer to its target and by how much: crater fields, regolith simulants, chambers, gravity offload. An infographic explains what Earth can never reproduce: pressure, radiation, gravity.
This helps space agencies choose and upgrade analog sites for astronaut training and hardware testing before Artemis and Mars missions.
details:
Earth Analog Explorer answers one question: which places on Earth best reproduce the conditions astronauts and hardware will face at specific sites on Mars and at the lunar south pole, and how can we close the remaining gap?

The core is a similarity index. Each site is described by eight measurable criteria: mean surface temperature, temperature range, crater density, mean slope, relief, ground ice fraction, maximum Sun elevation and rock type. Values are normalized (temperature as a ratio in kelvin, ice and crater density on log scales) and compared with weighted distances. Weights depend on the mission scenario: a lunar base prioritizes ice and illumination, a Mars landing prioritizes slope, relief and rock.

We compare 12 Earth analogs (Namib dunes and gravel plains, Roter Kamm crater, four McMurdo Dry Valleys sites, Haughton crater, the Devon Island plateau, the Fosheim Peninsula, and two Mistastin crater sites) with six references: Jezero, Gale and the Phoenix site on Mars; the Shackleton rim, the Shackleton floor and Malapert on the Moon.

The interface has four parts:

  • 3D globe and maps. Click an analog to fly to it, then compare it side by side with its Mars or Moon target.
  • Analysis. Rankings, radar charts per criterion, a heat map and raw-parameter comparisons.
  • Close the gap. A what-if simulator. It applies interventions (artificial crater fields, regolith simulant test beds, graded slopes, thermal-vacuum and Mars chambers, gravity offload) and recalculates the score live, ranking them by gain per effort.
  • “Can humans live here?” infographic. Pressure and radiation on log scales, a liquid-water phase window, available solar power, and a survival kit of what Earth can never provide.

Benefits

  • It turns “this place looks like Mars” into a transparent, reproducible number, and shows which criteria match and which don’t.
  • It separates what can be fixed in the field, what needs chambers and what is impossible on Earth (vacuum, radiation, gravity).
  • Every value carries a status badge (literature, computed, estimate), so users see what is measured and what still needs verification.

Expected impact

Agencies and research teams can use it to choose analog sites for astronaut training and hardware testing, and to decide which upgrades give the biggest improvement for the effort. That matters before Artemis surface missions and future crewed Mars missions. The open data format lets anyone add new sites or criteria.

Tools and technologies

  • Front end: HTML, CSS, JavaScript; globe.gl (three.js) for 3D globes, Leaflet for maps, Chart.js for charts, Papa Parse for CSV, html2canvas for PNG export.
  • Analysis: Python (pandas, NumPy). Scripts compute the similarity scores, habitability parameters and what-if results, plus an automated consistency check (CHECKS.md) that verifies data integrity and reproducibility.
  • Physics: Sun elevation from latitude and axial tilt; liquid-water window from the vapor-pressure curve (Buck equation); top-of-atmosphere solar flux; gravity offload fractions.
  • Data: published NASA mission data and peer-reviewed literature (LRO illumination studies, MSL RAD, LCROSS, Phoenix), plus partner resources from ESA, CSA and JAXA.
  • Hardware: none. It is a static website that runs in any browser.
  • An AI assistant (Claude) helped with code generation and data checks; the team reviewed all data and decisions.

Creativity

Most analog work stops at “site X resembles Mars.” We made the gap itself the product: the tool measures how far each analog is from its target and simulates how to bring it closer, with real precedents such as the Cinder Lake crater field used for Apollo training. Pairing every Earth site with a specific landing site, rather than with “Mars in general,” makes the comparison concrete.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: known limits of the analogy are shown explicitly, and unverified values are flagged.
  • Scale mismatches, e.g. metre-scale artificial craters versus kilometre-scale crater statistics.
  • Seasonal effects: low polar Sun, peak versus mean temperatures.
  • Accessibility: English/Ukrainian interface, mobile layout, reduced-motion support and a 2D fallback without WebGL.
  • Reproducibility: one source data file, and every chart is generated from data, with no hard-coded numbers.
